claims.text: Local chemical ordering fluctuations in concentrated alloys create spatial variations in shear-fault energies.
Local chemical ordering pins dislocations by increasing lattice friction.
Local chemical ordering is a governing cause of strength and deformation behavior in concentrated alloys.
NiCoCr can exhibit appreciable local chemical or short-range order whose degree depends on processing history.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi can exhibit appreciable short-range or local chemical order due to typical processing history.
Controlled heat treatment can enhance or alter local chemical ordering.
Severe plastic deformation reduces local chemical order toward a random solid solution.
Homogenization can be used to enhance local chemical order.
L11- and L12-like short-range-order motifs occur in CrCoNi nanoclusters.
Locally ordered regions or chemical clusters act as dislocation-pinning sites and create a rugged energy landscape.
Enhanced local chemical order increases fluctuations in local shear-fault energies and raises activation barriers for dislocation activity.
Nanoscale dislocation-segment detrapping is a mechanism by which local chemical order increases lattice friction.
Enhanced local chemical order causes wavy dislocation paths.
Increasing short-range or local chemical order increases alloy strength.
A near-random solid solution has a smoother energy landscape in which dislocations move more freely.
An LCO-enhanced state will have higher yield strength than an LCO-minimized state of the same alloy.
An LCO-enhanced state will exhibit more irregular, pinned, wavy, or jumpy dislocation motion than an LCO-minimized state.
An LCO-minimized state will exhibit more uniform dislocation slip.
High-temperature homogenization can produce a near-random solid solution suitable as the LCO-minimized baseline.
The proposed mechanism should hold from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and across strain rates where dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates.

contradictions.description: Homogenization is presented in the intervention as an example of processing that enhances LCO, but high-temperature homogenization is presented in the baseline as a method that minimizes LCO and produces a near-random state. The temperature-dependent distinction is not specified clearly enough to resolve this inconsistency.
